text: A dry wind comes up the creek, carrying the end of a chant — words you almost understand, a rhythm like a heartbeat counted aloud. It stops mid-line, as though the chanter had walked indoors. The red lotuses at your feet tremble.

The tongueless bronze bell tugs once in a wind you cannot feel. Beneath the branch it hangs from, one blood-lotus bud — thicker, darker, folded past folded — does not answer the water at all. It seems to be listening. When you stop moving, the listening is louder.

The pond's surface settles. For a moment, in the red water, you do not see yourself — you see someone who looks almost like you but older, in robes the colour of the water, smiling with a mouth that has learned a new shape. Then the image is gone, and the pond is only a pond again.

Somewhere behind the gallery's north column, Weilan is grinding something. The mortar taps out a slow, familiar three — one-two, pause, one — and he hums across the pestle in a voice that has no words in it and does not need any. When the tune breaks, so does his rhythm; a moment later they both resume, the tune a half-step lower, as if it has been carrying a small weight and shifted it to the other hand.
